explanations: terra: A غِشَـٰوَةٌ lies over sight after hearts and hearing are sealed, internalizing the covering used in the section to avoid seeing and hearing truth.
terra: People put fingers in their ears against thunderclaps from fear of death, repeating Noah's hearers' exact bodily gesture in a storm rather than in response to preaching.

luna: The command to guard yourselves from the Fire (فَاتَّقُوا النَّارَ) makes taqwa a response to the very danger against which the section’s inner garment protects. | terra: فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ makes the taqwa verb itself the commanded protection from fire, the exact relation the section draws between 92:5 and the flame.
terra: True righteousness includes giving loved wealth to vulnerable people and ends by naming such people the muttaqin, directly coupling gift with taqwa.

luna: Spouses are described as garments for one another (هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَّهُنَّ), extending clothing from display to mutual closeness and covering. | terra: In the setting of the fasting night, spouses are called reciprocal clothing, هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَّهُنَّ, combining night, bodily enclosure, intimacy, and concealment.
terra: The command to spend is immediately joined to the warning not to cast oneself into destruction, directly coupling giving with avoidance of the fatal fall.

luna: The ayah calls taqwa the best provision (خَيْرَ الزَّادِ التَّقْوَىٰ); the section’s hidden garment can thus be read as what one carries for the way ahead. | terra: The best provision is taqwa, another Quranic image of inward protection as something carried for a journey rather than worn for display.

luna: The supplication asks God to protect its speakers from the punishment of the Fire (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), making taqwa’s protective root an explicit plea for safety. | terra: The prayer وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ asks for precisely the protection from fire that the section's taqwa-garment supplies.
terra: A good loan to Allah is multiplied many times, reversing the dictionary's robe-as-debt by making relinquished wealth a lasting credit.
terra: Charity displayed for people is like dust stripped from a rock and yields nothing, a precise image of an impressive outer layer with no protective inner substance.
terra: Spending for Allah's pleasure and from inner certainty is likened to a fruitful garden, supplying the inward counterpart to the showy spending stripped bare in 2:264.
terra: Concealed alms to the poor are better and erase evils, directly favoring a hidden protective good over visible display.
terra: Good expenditure benefits the giver and is made only in seeking Allah's Face, identifying the hidden intention beneath the source section's generous act.
terra: Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and publicly, bring the section's night-cover, hidden inner act, and giving into one formulation.

luna: The source section’s dictionary branch gives “debt” as a sense of ridā; this ayah treats a debtor in hardship and urges respite, making that secondary debt-as-mantle sense concrete as an obligation one bears. | terra: A debtor in hardship is to receive respite, and remission is better charity; this treats debt as a burden relieved by giving rather than an adornment retained.

luna: The source section’s dictionary branch gives debt as a secondary sense of ridā; this ayah treats a debt as a specified obligation to be recorded, so the link is that secondary debt-as-mantle sense, not a Quranic garment image. | terra: Because dayn is only the source dictionary's secondary sense of ridā, the command to record a fixed-term debt supplies a semantic boundary: the obligation remains real even when not outwardly visible.
terra: Wealth and children will not avail against Allah, and their owners become fuel for the Fire, joining failed possessions to the threatened flame in one ayah.
luna: The ayah lists gold, silver, livestock and fields among desires made attractive to people, giving specific material contents to the section’s adornment-like mantle.
luna: This neighbour answers the desires listed in 3:14 with what is better for the God-fearing, completing the contrast between worldly adornment and inner taqwa.

luna: Believers ask, “protect us from the punishment of the Fire” (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), matching the inner safeguard to the section’s fire scene. | terra: Believers ask وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, keeping the protection root and fire in the same short plea.
terra: People will not attain righteousness until they spend from what they love, placing inner moral gain in surrendering the would-be ornament.

luna: For those who disbelieve, neither wealth nor children will avail them against God, and they belong to the Fire; material support fails precisely at the section’s fire boundary. | terra: The same no-avail formula for wealth and children ends with abiding in the Fire, a direct parallel to the section's useless robe at destruction.

luna: The command to guard against the Fire prepared for disbelievers repeats the section’s protective verb and places it at the boundary of punishment. | terra: وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ again directly names taqwa as protection against a prepared fire.
terra: The Garden is prepared for the muttaqin, and the next ayah identifies them through spending, making taqwa the protection beneath generosity.
terra: Those who spend in ease and hardship are the muttaqin introduced in 3:133, a direct parallel to the section's giver who practices taqwa.
terra: Whoever defrauds will carry what was taken on Resurrection, turning secretly acquired wealth into a bodily borne liability rather than protective adornment.
terra: What misers withheld will be طَوَّقُوا۟, collared around their necks on Resurrection; hoarded wealth becomes the fatal thing worn on the body.

luna: The people of understanding likewise ask to be protected from the Fire (فَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), a repeated formulation of the safeguard named in the section. | terra: Those who remember and reflect conclude فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, showing the inward stance that seeks the true covering.
terra: Those who consume orphans' wealth eat fire into their bellies, turning acquired property into an inward burning rather than an inward protection.
terra: Spending to be seen by people supplies the outward act without faith, the opposite of the section's quiet inner layer of giving and taqwa.
terra: Within the covenant, establishing prayer and alms is joined to lending Allah a good loan, placing the debt image on the side of generous fidelity.
terra: Some listen while coverings on their hearts and heaviness in their ears prevent understanding, restaging the blocked hearing of Noah's clothed hearers inwardly.

luna: Night comes over Abraham (جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ) as he observes the star; this is a non-lexical scene of night enveloping a person, like the section’s night as an entered garment. | terra: When night جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ, Abraham is enclosed by it before seeing the star; the ayah makes the human viewpoint inside the night-cover perceptible.
luna: People come to God alone and leave behind what they were given; this pictures the loss of worldly goods when the self stands exposed.
terra: Allah appoints night for repose while breaking open the dawn, giving the section's night-garment a concrete function as an enclosing interval of rest.

luna: After the fall, Adam and his spouse begin fastening leaves from the Garden over themselves (مِن وَرَقِ الْجَنَّةِ); the scene makes clothing a response to exposure and loss. | terra: After the fall, Adam and his spouse fasten garden leaves over their exposed bodies; this is the loss-of-covering scene that immediately precedes 7:26's two garments.

luna: The ayah names “the garment of taqwa” (لِبَاسُ التَّقْوَى) as better than bodily clothing, directly naming the section’s unseen protective layer. | terra: The ayah first gives clothing for nakedness and adornment, then declares لِبَاسُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ better, explicitly joining the section's outer robe and inward protective layer.
terra: Satan strips the first parents of their clothing to expose them, setting the loss of an outer cover against the better taqwa-garment named in 7:26.

luna: The command to take one’s adornment at every place of prayer brings clothing into a setting of worship, a specific counterpoint to adornment carried as worldly display. | terra: People are told to take their adornment at worship but not be excessive, providing a boundary in which outward dress is legitimate without becoming self-sufficient display.

luna: This neighbour to 7:31 asks who forbade God’s adornment and good provisions; it clarifies that adornment can be a divine provision even while the section questions reliance on it. | terra: Allah's adornment and good provisions are not forbidden, but are purely for believers in the Hereafter, distinguishing gifted beauty from the false protective use of ornament.

luna: Hell is their bed with coverings above them; this root-related covering is a punishment, the boundary opposite the protective cover in the section. | terra: Hell is a bed with غَوَاشٍ above its people, converting an enclosing cover into punishment rather than shelter.

luna: The ayah says God covers the day with night (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), repeating the section’s root for night as an enveloping cover. | terra: Allah يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ, presenting night as a cover drawn over day rather than merely a time after it.
terra: Allah makes drowsiness يَغْشِّيكُم as security and follows it with purification and strengthened hearts, a benevolent covering that genuinely protects inwardly.

luna: The verse condemns hoarding gold and silver instead of spending in God’s path, turning the section’s showy wealth toward the fire punishment described immediately after. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend receive a warning of punishment, directly opposing the giver whose inward garment is taqwa.

luna: The hoarded gold and silver are heated in Hell’s fire and brand foreheads, sides and backs; ornament becomes an instrument of exposure and punishment. | terra: The hoarded metal from 9:34 is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, turning carried wealth into a fiery covering on the body.
terra: Some Bedouins regard expenditure as a financial burden and await misfortune, exposing the miser's construal of giving as debt.
terra: Others regard expenditure as nearness to Allah and the Messenger's prayers, reversing 9:98's burden and clarifying what giving can become inwardly.
terra: Charity taken from wealth purifies and causes growth, explaining how giving possessions supplies an inward cleansing rather than an outward ornament.

luna: A structure founded on taqwa is better than one on a crumbling brink; the foundation gives another image of the quiet support the section assigns to protection. | terra: A building founded on a crumbling edge collapses with its builder into Hellfire, a nonlexical staging of support and self-made security becoming a fall.

luna: The earth puts on its adornment, its people think they control it, then it is cut down as if it had not flourished; this sharply stages ornament, false security and its disappearance. | terra: The earth takes on its adornment and its people think they control it just before Allah's command leaves it mown down, a large-scale version of ornament mistaken for security.

luna: The faces of those who earned evil are covered with pieces of dark night (أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ); the same covering root becomes a sign of disgrace rather than shelter. | terra: Faces appear covered with pieces of dark night; the benign cosmic garment becomes an image of disgrace from which there is no protector.
terra: Night is made so people may rest in it and day so they may see, clarifying what the benign night-cover enables.
terra: Moses says Pharaoh and his chiefs were given adornment and wealth in worldly life and used it to lead astray, joining visible finery, possession, and moral ruin.

luna: The section quotes people wrapping themselves in garments (يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيَابَهُمْ) to hide, while the ayah says God knows both what they conceal and disclose. | terra: The exact source-section gesture appears: people يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيَابَهُمْ while trying to conceal themselves, yet Allah knows their secret and public speech.
terra: Those who want worldly life and its adornment can receive their works there, identifying the decorative object whose final failure 11:16 reveals.
terra: Those who wanted worldly life and its adornment in 11:15 have only the Fire in the Hereafter, exposing ornamental success as a garment that cannot endure.
terra: A غَاشِيَةٌ of Allah's punishment may come suddenly, using the covering root for an overwhelming threat rather than protective clothing.

luna: Here too the night covers the day (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), another direct occurrence of the section’s night-covering root. | terra: The repeated formula يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ supplies another direct cosmic staging of the section's night-cover.
terra: Those who seek their Lord's Face spend secretly and publicly and repel evil with good, joining concealed generosity to moral protection.
terra: The Hereafter's punishment is harder and there is no وَاقٍ from Allah, marking the limit beyond which no self-chosen covering can protect.
terra: Believers are commanded to spend secretly and publicly before a Day when trade cannot help, distinguishing present giving from wealth that later fails.

luna: The criminals’ shirts are of tar (سَرَابِيلُهُم مِّن قَطِرَانٍ) as fire covers their faces, reversing clothing’s ordinary protection into part of punishment. | terra: Their shirts are pitch and fire covers their faces, the source section's explicit inverse garment: what is worn and what covers both intensify the burning.
luna: Horses, mules and donkeys are given for riding and as adornment (وَزِينَةً), making the section’s broad dictionary gloss of adornment concrete in worldly possessions.

luna: People extract ornaments from the sea “which you wear” (حِلْيَةً تَلْبَسُونَهَا), a direct instance of beauty literally carried on the body. | terra: People extract ornaments from the sea that they wear, supplying a literal Quranic instance of material provision becoming bodily adornment like the source dictionary's robe.

luna: God provides shirts that protect from heat and battle (سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ), a bodily instance of the protective function the section reads within taqwa. | terra: The shirts تَقِيكُمُ heat and armor protects in battle; this is the section's literal Quranic meeting of a garment with the protecting sense of و ق ي.
terra: What people possess runs out while what is with Allah remains, stating the temporal difference between the failing worn ornament and genuine security.
terra: Allah makes a secure, well-provided town taste لِبَاسَ ٱلْجُوعِ وَٱلْخَوْفِ, showing that a garment can also be an enveloping punishment after ingratitude.
terra: Coverings on hearts and heaviness in ears culminate in people turning their backs when the one Lord is mentioned, closely matching concealment joined to turning away.
luna: What is on earth is made its adornment as a test of who does best in deed, making outward ornament answer to the inward measure of action.
terra: The Prophet is told not to let his eyes pass beyond sincere worshippers seeking the adornment of worldly life, preferring the hidden orientation over visible finery.
luna: The Fire’s pavilion surrounds its people, turning an enclosing cover into confinement and punishment rather than shelter.
terra: The righteous are adorned and wear green silk in the lasting Garden, a bestowed robe that contrasts with wealth worn as self-made worldly security.
terra: The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, giving voice to the self-sufficient stance beneath the decorative robe.
terra: The rich garden owner enters his estate while wronging himself and asserts that it will never perish, explicitly treating displayed wealth as lasting protection.
terra: He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return if brought back, extending the false security of his ornament beyond death.
terra: His companion tells him to acknowledge Allah's will and that there is no power except through Allah, naming the stance absent from the self-worn robe.

luna: The garden owner’s wealth is ruined, and he wrings his hands over what he spent; the failed property gives a concrete counterpart to wealth that cannot save its owner. | terra: His produce is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while the trellises lie collapsed, making prosperous display end in visible downfall.
terra: No company can help the ruined owner besides Allah and he cannot defend himself, stating why the collapsed wealth of 18:42 was no covering.

luna: Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better; this distinguishes the showy mantle from what remains. | terra: Wealth and children are زِينَةُ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا while lasting deeds are better, precisely distinguishing the decorative robe from what remains.
terra: One reminded of the signs turns away, while coverings lie over hearts and heaviness in ears; it is a nonliteral counterpart to the source's clothed evasion of warning.
terra: Allah saves those who practiced taqwa and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling in Hell, matching the inward garment's actual rescue from the flame.
terra: Moses is warned not to be turned from the Hour فَتَرْدَىٰ, using the source root in its ruin/perishing sense and tying that ruin to heedless desire.

luna: The sea overtakes Pharaoh’s people (فَغَشِيَهُم مِّنَ الْيَمِّ), using the section’s covering root for a fatal engulfing rather than a protective wrap. | terra: The sea فَغَشِيَهُم with what covered them, using the covering root for a fatal engulfing instead of shelter.
terra: Paradise is promised as a place where Adam will not be naked, preparing the covering-loss scene in 20:121.
terra: Adam will not suffer the sun's heat in Paradise, identifying the exposure from which clothing protects before the fall.
terra: After disobedience, the pair's nakedness appears and they patch on garden leaves, repeating the fall-and-cover scene behind 7:22-26.
terra: The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the flower of worldly life; his Lord's provision is better and more lasting, another boundary around decorative possession.
luna: The disbelievers will be unable to ward the Fire from their faces or backs; this states the limit of every bodily defense against the fire the section warns of.

luna: David is taught to make armor that protects people from their own violence (لِتُحْصِنَكُم مِّن بَأْسِكُمْ), a direct bodily garment of protection. | terra: Allah teaches David the making of لَبُوسٍ that protects people from violence, an unambiguous garment whose value lies in protection rather than display.
terra: Those for whom good has preceded are kept far from Hell, a nonlexical equivalent of the section's most protected person being spared the flame.

luna: This ayah clothes the disputing unbelievers in garments of fire; the garment that should cover and protect instead belongs to the section’s warned-of fire. | terra: ثِيَابٌ مِّن نَّارٍ are cut out for the disputants, turning the protective function of clothing into its exact opposite.
terra: Believers are adorned with gold and pearls and their clothing is silk, locating true outward adornment after divine entry into the Garden.
terra: One who associates partners is likened to a person falling from the sky and being snatched or swept away, a nonlexical picture of the source root's fatal descent.
luna: The ayah says revering God’s signs comes from taqwa of hearts (مِن تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ), joining a visible practice to an inward layer.

luna: The flesh and blood of sacrifice do not reach God, but taqwa does; this separates the unseen inward layer from visible material offering. | terra: Neither sacrificial flesh nor blood reaches Allah, but taqwa from people does, sharply distinguishing the unseen inward reality from a visible material form.

luna: The women are told to draw their head-coverings over their bosoms (بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلَىٰ جُيُوبِهِنَّ); this gives the section’s clothing image a bodily act of covering. | terra: Drawing head-coverings over the bosom and not displaying adornment joins a worn cover to the concealment of ornament, clarifying the section's quiet layer beneath show.
terra: A wave يَغْشَىٰهُ another wave with cloud above produces darkness upon darkness, a layered natural covering that helps picture the section's hidden intermediate layer.
terra: Older women may set aside outer garments without displaying adornment, yet restraint is better; the ayah marks a boundary between the garment itself and the inward quality.

luna: Night is made a garment, sleep a rest, and day a rising; the verse joins the section’s covering image to the night/day passage of the surah. | terra: Allah again makes night a garment, then pairs it with sleep and the day's rising, giving the section's worn night-cover its daily function.

luna: On the Day, wealth and children do not avail; this directly sharpens the section’s claim about wealth at the moment of downfall. | terra: The Day when neither wealth nor children benefit states the same boundary on material protection without staging the fall itself.
luna: This neighbour supplies the exception to 26:88: what avails is coming to God with a sound heart, setting inward condition against wealth and children.
terra: Allah saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from the destroyed settlement, showing taqwa's protective result in an earthly judgment.
terra: The repeated sign of night for rest and day for visibility places covering darkness and exposure to sight in a purposeful pair.

luna: What people receive is “enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment,” while what is with God is better and more lasting, directly testing the section’s garment-as-ornament image. | terra: Worldly gifts are enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting, setting the robe's passing glitter against what endures.
terra: The question who could bring night in which people rest if day were perpetual marks the life-giving boundary supplied by the night-cover.
terra: Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company, making his wealth physically weighty before it appears publicly as adornment.
terra: Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, voicing the self-sufficiency behind the ornament displayed in 28:79.

luna: Qarun comes before his people “in his adornment” (فِي زِينَتِهِ), staging the display of wealth that the section hears as a mantle carried on the shoulder. | terra: Qarun comes before his people فِى زِينَتِهِۦ, making wealth's public display into the visible ornamental robe imagined by the section.
terra: Those given knowledge answer the spectators of Qarun's adornment that Allah's reward is better for believers who act rightly.

luna: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no group can help him; the adornment of the preceding scene offers no protection when it is time to fall. | terra: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no company can protect him; the adornment of 28:79 fails at the precise moment of downfall.

luna: After Qarun’s fall, the people who had wished for his position recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the neighbour interprets the failed display as no secure measure of worth. | terra: After Qarun's fall, yesterday's admirers recognize that wealth's expansion is Allah's test and that unbelievers do not prosper, stating the scene's correction.

luna: Those who take protectors besides God are compared to a spider taking a house, the weakest of houses; the ayah pictures a shelter that cannot perform the protection the section assigns to taqwa.
terra: Hell already encompasses the unbelievers before 29:55 depicts punishment covering them from above and below, completing the anti-garment enclosure.
terra: Punishment يَغْشَىٰهُم from above and beneath their feet, an all-enclosing anti-garment.
terra: A gift intended to increase through people brings no increase with Allah, while alms seeking His Face multiplies, separating outward financial return from inwardly directed giving.

luna: The women draw their outer garments close, with the stated result that they may be recognized and not harmed; clothing here has a protective social function. | terra: Women are told to draw their outer cloaks close so they may be recognized and not harmed, giving the jilbab a concrete protective role akin to the source dictionary's vikāya layer.

luna: David is told to make full coats of mail and then to do good; the ayah joins protective clothing with moral action, as the section joins garment and taqwa. | terra: David is told to make full coats of mail and measure their links, supplying the crafted layers of the protective clothing whose purpose 21:80 states.
terra: The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, explicitly treating possessions as a shield.
terra: Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to Allah; faith and good action do, separating outward possession from the inward basis of safety.
terra: The repeated sea scene yields ornaments that people wear, concretizing the section's secondary definition of whatever adorns a person as their robe.
terra: Those who spend secretly and publicly hope for a commerce that never perishes, converting relinquished wealth into the lasting asset the decorative robe cannot be.
terra: The people entering the everlasting Garden receive bracelets, pearls, and silk garments, another robe bestowed after salvation rather than relied on before it.
terra: Allah فَأَغْشَيْنَـٰهُمْ so they cannot see; the self-chosen garment of refusal becomes a divinely imposed covering of perception.

luna: Daylight is stripped from night, leaving people in darkness; this gives the night/day pair a clothing-removal image complementary to night as covering. | terra: Day is stripped نَسْلَخُ from night and people are left in darkness, a garment-like removal that complements night being laid over the world.
terra: A person in Paradise tells his former companion إِن كِدتَّ لَتُرْدِينِ, using the same root for nearly bringing someone to ruin through denial.

luna: Night and day are repeatedly wrapped around one another (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ), extending the image from a garment to the alternating world. | terra: Allah يُكَوِّرُ night over day and day over night, using the action of wrapping one layer around another to stage the cosmic garment nonlexically.

luna: Canopies of fire above and below become an enclosing covering with no shelter, reversing the section’s image of a quiet protective layer. | terra: Layers of fire stand above and below Hell's people, a complete fiery enclosure opposed to the unseen cloth that guards from flame.
terra: The condemned person can only يَتَّقِى بِوَجْهِهِۦ the terrible punishment, a bitter reversal in which the exposed face must serve as an inadequate shield.
terra: Allah delivers those who had taqwa so that evil does not touch them, stating the protective efficacy that the source section renders as an unseen cloth.
terra: The angels ask Allah to وَقِهِمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, using the source root for direct protection from Hell.

luna: The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds (وَقِهِمُ السَّيِّئَاتِ), extending the section’s protective root from bodily danger to moral harm. | terra: The prayer وَقِهِمُ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ then defines such protection on that Day as mercy, bringing out the inward moral work of the section's vikāya.
terra: Earlier peoples had greater strength and monuments, yet Allah seized them and they had no protector, joining failed outward power to the absence of true vikāya.
terra: On the Day people turn their backs fleeing, no one can protect them from Allah, setting a boundary on every merely external defense.
terra: Allah protects the believer from the evils of Pharaoh's plot, while the punishment surrounds Pharaoh's people, showing effective protection immediately before their fire scene.
terra: Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, specifying the danger from which the believer of 40:45 was protected.
terra: Allah again makes night for rest and day for sight, presenting darkness as a provided shelter rather than mere absence of light.
terra: Rejecters answer the messenger that their hearts are in coverings, their ears heavy, and a barrier stands between them, verbalizing the refusal enacted by wrapping in clothes.
terra: Those who believed and practiced taqwa are rescued from the punishing blast, another concrete deliverance attributed to the inward stance.
terra: The false assumption people held about their Lord أَرْدَىٰكُمْ, ruined them, showing an inward cause of the downfall named by the source root.

luna: Even silver roofs, stairs, doors and couches would be only worldly enjoyment, while the Hereafter is with the God-fearing; material ornament is bounded against taqwa. | terra: After listing lavish fittings, the ayah calls them mere worldly زُخْرُفًا and reserves the Hereafter for the muttaqin, directly opposing ornament to taqwa.
terra: Pharaoh demands to know why Moses has not been given gold bracelets or an angelic retinue, treating worn ornament as proof of authority.
terra: After Pharaoh's display-based challenge, Allah drowns him and his people, showing the impotence of the status ornament invoked in 43:53.
luna: The God-fearing are placed in a secure station (مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ), directly linking taqwa to safety.
luna: The people identified as God-fearing in 44:51 wear silk and brocade; this ayah places clothing within the secure reward of the protected, rather than the failed worldly mantle.

luna: This parallel promise also says God protects them from Hell’s punishment (وَوَقَاهُمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ), linking taqwa’s safety to the section’s fire boundary. | terra: The people of the Garden are وَوَقَىٰهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, explicitly protected by Allah from Hell with the section's protection root.
terra: Allah places غِشَـٰوَةً over the sight of one who takes desire as a god, presenting perceptual covering as the result of inward self-sufficiency.
luna: God binds the believers to the word of taqwa (وَأَلْزَمَهُمْ كَلِمَةَ التَّقْوَىٰ) after placing tranquility in their hearts, locating the section’s protective quality inwardly.
terra: The most honored person before Allah is the most possessed of taqwa, relocating distinction from visible status and adornment to the inward quality.

luna: The Lord protects the Garden’s people from the punishment of Hell (وَوَقَاهُمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ), giving the protective root its final-fire setting. | terra: Amid their enjoyment, their Lord وَوَقَىٰهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, making rescue from flame the ground beneath the visible reward.
terra: The saved say Allah favored them and وَوَقَىٰنَا عَذَابَ ٱلسَّمُومِ, a first-person statement of the protective layer against scorching punishment.
terra: The question whether the hearers are مُّثْقَلُونَ مِن مَّغْرَمٍ pictures an imposed payment as weight, giving concrete force to the source dictionary's debt worn like a robe.
luna: God is the one who enriches and grants sufficiency (هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ), reversing the miser’s belief that his own wealth makes him self-sufficient.
terra: What covered the overturned towns covered them utterly; although the wording leaves the agent undescribed, the source root again denotes a fatal covering.
terra: The question who will lend Allah a good loan promises multiplication and a noble reward, again transforming wealth from carried liability into gift.
terra: Charitable men and women are described as lending Allah a good loan that is multiplied, turning parted wealth into credit rather than carrying it as liability.

luna: Worldly life is described as play, adornment and boasting, then vegetation withers and crumbles; the scene makes visible the passing quality of the ornament worn by the self-sufficient. | terra: Worldly life is described as adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before becoming dry debris, exposing the short life of the robe made from possessions.

luna: The ayah repeats that wealth and children will not avail against God and places their owners among the Fire’s people, another direct reversal of wealth as supposed shelter. | terra: Neither wealth nor children avail against Allah, and the people concerned are companions of the Fire; possession supplies no protective layer.
terra: Those who prefer others despite need are يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ, so generosity itself discloses an inward protection from possessiveness.
luna: The warning not to let wealth or children distract from God’s remembrance connects material attachment to the section’s image of wrapping oneself away from a warning.
terra: The ayah joins taqwa, listening, obedience, spending, and being يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ; protection here is specifically protection from the avarice of the section's miser.
terra: Following the command to spend and the protection from avarice in 64:16, a good loan to Allah is multiplied and forgiven; giving reverses the source dictionary's robe-as-debt.
luna: Whoever has taqwa is given a way out (يَجْعَل لَّهُ مَخْرَجًا), a specific result of the inner safeguard that parallels the section’s promise of ease.

luna: “Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire” (قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا) states the safeguarding action named by the section’s root و ق ي. | terra: قُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا commands active protection from fire with the same و ق ي root that the section hears as a protective cloth.
terra: The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them, giving a concrete form to the withholding stance of the section's miser.
terra: On finding their garden ruined, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived, reversing the security they sought by excluding the poor.
terra: The repeated phrase مُّثْقَلُونَ مِن مَّغْرَمٍ again makes liability something that weighs a person down, close to the section's shoulder-borne debt image.

luna: The speaker says, “My wealth did not avail me” (مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ), almost exactly the section’s claim that wealth gives no gain at the moment of falling. | terra: The condemned speaker says مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ, almost exactly restaging the section's claim that wealth avails nothing at the fall.

luna: After the speaker says in 69:28 that his wealth did not avail him, this ayah adds that his authority is gone, completing the loss of worldly support. | terra: The speaker's authority has perished immediately after his wealth avails nothing in 69:28, extending the failure from possession to status.
terra: The speaker whose wealth and authority failed is seized and shackled, so his former possessions end in an imposed bodily binding.
terra: He is then burned in Hell, completing the movement from failed wealth in 69:28 to the fire against which it supplied no cover.
terra: The passage identifies failure to urge feeding the poor among the condemned man's offenses, linking his useless wealth to withheld generosity.
terra: The blaze identified in 70:15 calls the one who gathered wealth and withheld it, reproducing the miser-to-fire movement behind the section's two garments.
terra: In the same passage where fire calls the collector who withheld, the prayerful have a recognized share within their wealth, presenting the opposite relation to possession.
terra: That fixed share belongs to the petitioner and deprived, specifying the giving that answers the hoarder's failure in 70:18.

luna: Nuh says his people put fingers in their ears and wrap themselves in garments (وَاسْتَغْشَوْا ثِيَابَهُمْ), an explicit act of clothing used to evade a warning. | terra: Noah's hearers block their ears and wrap themselves in their clothes, so the garment concretely becomes refusal of the warner.

luna: The “wrapped one” (الْمُزَّمِّلُ) is addressed while clothed, but this address opens a call to rise for night worship rather than wrap oneself to evade a warning. | terra: The address يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُزَّمِّلُ presents a person physically enwrapped, the human-scale counterpart to the section's night worn as a garment.

luna: This neighbour completes 73:1’s wrapped figure by telling him to rise during the night; the garmented stance leads to response, unlike wrapping to avoid admonition. | terra: The enwrapped person of 73:1 is commanded to rise in the night, so entering the night-cover becomes wakeful obedience rather than concealment from a warning.
terra: The surah of the enwrapped night-worshipper ends by joining alms with a good loan to Allah, uniting night, garment, gift, and the section's debt-sense of the robe.

luna: The “one who covers himself” (الْمُدَّثِّرُ) is directly addressed, echoing the section’s self-wrapping scene before the command that follows turns him outward. | terra: The address يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُدَّثِّرُ likewise begins with a cloaked person and makes the posture of being wrapped morally open to what follows.

luna: This neighbour completes the covered address in 74:1 with “rise and warn” (قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ), reversing clothing as a way of withdrawing from warning. | terra: The cloaked person of 74:1 is told قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ, reversing the people who wrap their garments to evade the warner.

luna: “Your garments, purify” (وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ) connects clothing to purification, giving the section’s inwardly clean protective garment a concrete parallel. | terra: وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ places the cleansing of garments beside the cloaked warner's commission, inviting the section's relation between outer dress and inward readiness without deciding the phrase's full scope.
terra: The cloaked warner is told not to give in pursuit of greater return, supplying an inward rule for giving beside the command to purify his garments.
terra: The people of Saqar admit they did not feed the poor, tying the fire announced in the cloaked warner's surah to withheld provision.
terra: Giving food despite love for it to the needy, orphan, and captive concretely enacts the generous wearer of the section's inward garment.
terra: The givers seek only Allah's Face and no repayment or thanks, identifying the unseen motive beneath the act in 76:8.
terra: Their fear of a grim Day supplies the taqwa-like inward stance that links the giving of 76:8-9 to protection.

luna: God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day (فَوَقَاهُمُ اللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ), a further instance of inward righteousness as safety. | terra: Allah وَقَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمِ, making protection the direct consequence of the preceding gift, intention, and fear.
terra: The protected givers are rewarded with Garden and silk, so a true outward garment follows the inward protection of 76:11.
terra: The saved are clothed in green silk and adorned with silver bracelets; following 76:8-12, visible dress arrives as gift after inward giving, fear, and protection.

luna: This ayah directly calls night a “garment” (لِبَاسًا), making explicit the section’s shift from night spread over the world to a person entering clothing. | terra: The ayah names night itself لِبَاسًا, exactly confirming the section's image of entering the night as one enters a garment.
terra: The rebuked people do not urge one another to feed the poor, giving a social form to the miser's refusal.
terra: They love wealth with consuming love, stating the inward attachment that turns possessions into the section's deceptive robe.
terra: Hell is brought into view after the rebuke over the poor and love of wealth, completing the same possession-to-fire sequence.

luna: The section’s named root غ ش و appears as night covering its counterpart, an exact verbal scene for the night that envelops. | terra: Night is sworn by إِذَا يَغْشَىٰهَا, repeating the source ayah's covering action while giving that action an object.
luna: The human transgresses “because he sees himself self-sufficient” (أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ), matching the section’s miser who carries wealth as if it made him sufficient.
luna: This neighbour completes the self-sufficiency claim in 96:7 by saying the return is to the Lord, setting a limit on the wealth-backed confidence.
luna: The opening ayah says rivalry in abundance distracts people; 102:2 names the grave as its endpoint, exposing the impermanence behind wealth as ornament.
luna: This ayah completes the accumulation that distracts in 102:1 with its endpoint, “until you visit the graves”; worldly abundance ends at death.
terra: The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth embodies the self-sufficient wearer of the section's ornamental robe.

luna: The hoarder “thinks his wealth will make him live forever” (يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ), exposing the false security of wealth as a mantle. | terra: He supposes his wealth has made him immortal, explicitly mistaking possessions for protection before the rejection in 104:4.
terra: The wealth-counter of 104:2-3 is cast into the Crusher, decisively breaking his belief that wealth preserves him.
terra: The Crusher of 104:4 is identified as Allah's kindled fire, completing the rich man's movement from counted wealth to flame.
terra: The kindled fire following the wealth-counter rises over the hearts, replacing the inward protective layer with inward-reaching flame.
terra: The fire is closed over its people, forming an imprisoning cover around the one who mistook accumulated wealth for security.
terra: Those who merely show their worship embody visible display without the inward protective quality the section assigns to taqwa.
terra: The show-offs of 107:6 also withhold small aid, joining outward appearance to the miser's refusal to give.

luna: Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings do not avail him (مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ), a direct counterpart to the section’s failed wealth. | terra: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ directly repeats the failure of a hostile rich man's wealth to protect him.

luna: This neighbour to the failed wealth in 111:2 names the flaming Fire (نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ), bringing the consequence into the same wealth-and-fire sequence. | terra: The man whose wealth fails in 111:2 enters a flaming fire, completing the same no-protection sequence as the source section.
terra: A fiber rope is around the neck of the household that trusted wealth, an exact bodily counter-image in which what is worn signifies liability and punishment.
